accuracy.evidence: Checked against DfE English Appendix 2, Year 4: the terms adverbial and fronted adverbial, fronted adverbials as a way to vary openings, and the comma after a fronted adverbial with the 'Later that day, I heard the bad news.' example. Every lab and quiz sentence puts the comma after the complete opener, never inside it, and keeps the capital letter on the opener.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the Year 4 slips teachers report: believing only -ly words are adverbials, putting the comma inside a multi-word opener (Later, that day), leaving it out, adding a comma between subject and verb (The owls, woke up), adding a comma when the adverbial stays at the end, and starting every sentence with a fronted adverbial.

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanism is moving a chunk: tap the when/where/how chunk, drag it to the front slot and watch the capital and comma appear, tap the comma gap, judge six sentences and sort openers into when, where and how. flagwhen builds time and cause conjunction clauses and flagrehearse varies whole sentence shapes; neither moves an adverbial or places a comma gap. The 30% shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: Feedback names the rule at the point of error: tapping 'The fox' says it tells who and the adverbial tells when or where; tapping 'crept' says it is the action; a wrong comma gap is drawn in red with 'Put the comma after the whole phrase'; judging 'The children, ran home after school.' as correct gives 'No opener here. Never put a comma between who did it and the verb.' Step summaries then restate each rule.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options: 'No, it is one word like "quickly"' is disproved when the phrase 'at midnight' is the answer; 'Nothing else' changes is disproved when the capital letter and comma appear as the chunk moves; the comma 'after Later' is disproved when the Later gap turns red and 'after day' is accepted.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The Challenge rotates questions on comma position, picking the fronted adverbial, which sentence needs no comma, and how versus when versus where, with tagged wrong-answer messages such as 'The comma splits "Later that day" in half', '"a bat" is who the sentence is about', '"Quietly" is a one-word opener. It still needs a comma' and 'Never put a comma between who did it and the verb.'

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences with concrete examples (the fox at midnight, the cat creeping, the children going home) and pass the learner FK limit in the content gate; adult paragraphs name the curriculum year, the adverbial forms and the common mistakes within the adult limit.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph does a job: the definition with three examples, moving the chunk, comma placement with a wrong example, varying openers; the adult text covers curriculum placement, phrase and clause adverbials, mistakes, and what the lab does. The content gate's filler and similarity checks passed.

mobile.evidence: Checked on a 360 px Android screenshot and an iPhone 13 run: the comma-gap sentence now shrinks its font to fit the width after an early version clipped 'bag.', chunk tiles wrap onto two rows, and every chunk, gap and bin also has a full-width button below the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: axe passed in light and dark themes in the browser gate; the canvas has an aria-label, every drag has a button alternative named for the action (Move "at midnight" to the front, after "breakfast"), and the bin colours pass contrast in both themes with icons as well as colour.

sources: Department for Education (2013), English Appendix 2: vocabulary, grammar and punctuation, Year 4 (fronted adverbials; commas after fronted adverbials; terminology: adverbial)
Department for Education (2013), English programmes of study: key stage 2, Years 3–4 writing composition (varied and rich vocabulary and an increasing range of sentence structures)
Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts, L.5.2b (use a comma to separate an introductory element from the rest of the sentence)
